Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Russia, claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 STATEMENT OF ALLEGED FACTS

The claimant was born in Russia, moved to Azerbaijan in 1977, received Azerbaijan citizenship and remained an Azerbaijan citizen. The claimant's counsel confirmed that Russia is not a country of reference. She was widowed in 1998. In 2003, she stated that she joined a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX) as a XXXXX. Her XXXXX work was XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX or from the XXXXX themselves about their XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. That is where her involvement ends. In 2004, the Chairperson of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX about the problems of the XXXXX XXXXX. As a result, the claimant stated that she started receiving threatening phone calls to stop her activities in the organization. In XXXXX 2005 she also testified that two police officers came to her house and took her to the police station where she was held overnight. She claimed that she was told to stop her work with the organization. In XXXXX 2006, the claimant went to Russia to attend to her ailing relative and came back to Azerbaijan after three months and continued to do her XXXXX work. In XXXXX 2007, she stated that she was assaulted by two women and was again told to cease her XXXXX work.
Fearing for her life, she fled Azerbaijan, arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2007 and filed her refugee protection claim on XXXXX, 2008. ANALYSIS Identity
I find that the claimant is a citizen of Russia. This has been established by prima facie evidence of her Russian passport and Canadian visitor visa.2 Determination

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee (based on her perceived political opinion) under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a person in need of protection under section 97 (1)(b) of the IRPA. Credibility
I find that the claimant did not provide credible and trustworthy evidence to support her claim.

The claimant testified that no identification card was issued to her as a XXXXX member, although the job assigned to her was to XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX or from the XXXXX themselves, who she did not know before. Her explanation was "most XXXXX would trust me." I find the claimant's testimony very unusual to the point of not being credible. It is reasonable to expect that an organization involved with the XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX for that matter would identify its XXXXX or XXXXX with identification cards. It is also reasonable to expect that XXXXX XXXXX or the XXXXX XXXXX would want to know who they were dealing with on matters of sensitive issues such as XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, through identification cards. The claimant's testimony that she went on XXXXX XXXXX information for XXXXX years from XXXXX she met for the first time with no identification card because "most XXXXX trusted her" reflects on the credibility of her story. This issue of identification card is so basic that her testimony impacts her overall credibility, given the nature of the work of her organization and considering her education and work experience as an XXXXX, XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX.

The claimant's testimony in her expedited hearing that she submitted an application to be a XXXXX was not consistent with the narrative to her Personal Information Form3 (PIF) where she stated that there was no application form to be completed to be a XXXXX of the organization. When asked to explain the apparent inconsistency, she stated that there was indeed an application form, because without it, she would not have been accepted into the organization. The claimant would not admit the PIF was incorrect.4 The claimant had no choice but to stand by her oral testimony. However, at the full hearing of her claim, when asked how she signed up as a XXXXX, she testified that she wrote a letter to XXXXX XXXXX (XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX). When asked if she received a response, she testified "No, I did not. I got a verbal answer that I could participate as a XXXXX." I draw an adverse credibility inference on the claimant's continuing conflicting testimony.

The organization she worked for was the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX 5 but she referred to it in her narrative on several instances as the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. Her explanation for calling it a different name was "I was talking about the association of XXXXX XXXXX, the roots of the organization and where it was derived from." I find the claimant's explanation nonsensical and not reasonable. There was no valid reason for her to refer to the organization with a different name of her own making, considering that she had to identify herself and the organization she worked for every time she XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX for the last XXXXX years. On a balance of probabilities, the claimant did not realize her referral to the organization with a different name. On a balance of probabilities, her explanation was an embellishment to diffuse her error in referring to the organization with a different name, where she was supposed to have worked for XXXXX years.

Her inconsistent testimony as regards to the process of becoming a XXXXX, her testimony as to the lack of an identification card and her lack of knowledge as to the correct name of the organization she allegedly worked for XXXXX years, are so basic that it belies her claim of working as a XXXXX for the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. Her unreasonable and inconsistent evidence do impact negatively on her credibility and ultimately on the well-foundedness of her alleged fear. Accordingly, I give her documentary evidence of her being a XXXXX with the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and the threats and physical assault on her as a result of her XXXXX work, very minimal probative value.

Since this panel has determined that the claimant's overall testimony is seriously lacking in credibility as to the material allegations of her claim, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under section 97(1)(b), as there is no risk to her life or a risk of unusual and cruel treatment or punishment, should she return to Azerbaijan. Conclusion

Based on the foregoing analysis and after considering the totality of the evidence, I find that there is not a reasonable chance or a serious possibility that the claimant will be persecuted for a Convention ground, if she were to return to Azerbaijan. I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant will not be subjected to a risk to her life, or a risk to cruel or unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, if she were to return to Azerbaijan. Her claim is rejected.
